claims.claim: Adjectives are words that modify, or give information about, nouns and pronouns; they answer questions such as which one, what kind, what color, and what shape.

An adjective can appear directly before the noun it modifies (attributive position), and it also follows forms of be and sense or appearance verbs such as feel, look, seem, taste, smell, sound, appear when it describes the subject (predicative position).

One-syllable adjectives form the comparative with -er and the superlative with -est (cheap, cheaper, cheapest); two-syllable adjectives ending in -y change y to i (busy, busier, busiest); adjectives of three or more syllables use more/less and most/least (more interesting, the most popular).

A few common adjectives have irregular comparative and superlative forms, including good/better/best and bad/worse/worst (also far/farther/farthest), and more or most must not be combined with an -er or -est form.

When more than one adjective precedes a noun, English normally follows a conventional order — opinion, size, age, shape, color, origin, material — with opinion adjectives first; the sequence is a guideline rather than a rigid rule, and fuller reference lists add categories such as physical quality, type, and purpose.

There are no general rules for which preposition follows which adjective; combinations such as interested in and good at must be learned together as pairs, and the preposition in such pairs is followed by a noun or a gerund.

Adjectives modify nouns, while adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs, so using an adjective where an adverb is required (for example, "the choir sang beautiful" for "the choir sang beautifully") is a common learner error; the full adverb rules belong to the sibling adverbs topic.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The number of categories in the conventional adjective order varies across references.
positions: Cambridge English Grammar Today lists ten categories: opinion, size, physical quality, shape, age, color, origin, material, type, purpose.
Many learner materials teach a shortened sequence of six or seven categories.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson teaches the shortened conventional sequence (opinion, size, age, shape, color, origin, material) as a guideline and notes that fuller reference lists add categories such as type and purpose.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the superlative may be used when only two things are compared.
positions: Grammar guides traditionally prescribe the comparative when a group has just two members (Cambridge: 'traditionally, we use the comparative').
Cambridge also notes that in informal usage people often use the superlative in such cases.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the traditional guideline (comparative for two, superlative for groups of three or more) and does not present informal usage as an error.

sourceRecords.title: Adjective or Adverb? — How to Use Adjectives and Adverbs
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A per the subject source map. Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports: adjectives modify nouns and adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs; an adjective follows a form of be (Rule #2) and follows sense/appearance verbs (feel, taste, smell, sound, look, appear, seem) when it modifies the noun before the verb (Rule #3); good is an adjective while well is an adverb ('you do well,' 'you feel good'); 'I feel bad' versus 'I feel badly'. Facts only; no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Parts of Speech: Part 2 — Building on Foundations — Language Foundations Handbook
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A per the subject source map (eCampusOntario Language Foundations Handbook). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports the definitions of modifier (a word, phrase, or clause that adds detail, limits, or clarifies), adjective (a word that describes a noun), adverb (a word that describes a verb, an adjective, or another adverb), and the treatment of articles as a type of adjective used before a noun. Facts only; no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Comparison: adjectives (bigger, biggest, more interesting) — English Grammar Today
sourceRecords.provider: Cambridge University Press and Assessment (Cambridge Dictionary)
sourceRecords.notes: Reputable reference grammar. Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports: comparative compares one person or thing with another and superlative compares with the whole group; -er/-est for one-syllable adjectives with the normally used before the superlative; two-syllable adjectives ending in -y change y to i and take -er/-est (busy, busier, busiest); adjectives of three or more syllables take more/less and most/least (more interesting, the most popular, the least expensive); irregular forms bad/worse/worst, good/better/best, far/farther/farthest; warning that more or most must not combine with -er/-est ('a more better life' is marked as not standard); for two-member groups the comparative is traditional while informal usage often uses the superlative. Facts only; no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Adjectives: order — English Grammar Today
sourceRecords.provider: Cambridge University Press and Assessment (Cambridge Dictionary)
sourceRecords.notes: Reputable reference grammar. Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports: when more than one adjective comes before a noun, the adjectives are normally in a particular order; opinion adjectives come first, before more neutral factual ones ('an amazing red coat,' not 'a red amazing coat'); the 'most usual sequence' table runs opinion, size, physical quality, shape, age, color, origin, material, type, purpose, with examples; the order is presented as the most usual sequence rather than an absolute rule. Facts only; no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Adjectives and prepositions — LearnEnglish
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B per the subject source map (British Council). The live host blocked automated access, so the page was read via an Internet Archive capture of 2022-05-20 (web.archive.org/web/20220520001939/https://learnenglish.britishcouncil.org/grammar/a1-a2-grammar/adjectives-and-prepositions). Supports: some adjectives go with certain prepositions; there are no grammatical rules for which preposition goes with which adjective, so they are best learned together; the preposition is followed by a noun or a gerund; examples include interested in, good at, worried about, afraid of, proud of, excited about. Facts only; no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: 2.5 Adjectives and Adverbs — Business Grammar
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B OER (open textbook; the same book's Chapter 2.1 is an existing registry source used by the parts-of-speech lesson). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports: adjectives modify only nouns and pronouns; an adjective answers questions such as which one, what kind, what color, and what shape; adjectives often come before the nouns they modify; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs; articles are treated as special types of adjectives that modify nouns and pronouns. Facts only; no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: 9.1 Choosing Between Adjectives and Adverbs — Business Grammar
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B OER. Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports: adjectives follow sense verbs such as feel and look ('They feel bad about the decision'); commonly confused adjective/adverb pairs with irregular spellings include good/well and bad/badly; the choice between adjective and adverb depends on whether the subject or the verb is being modified. Facts only; no wording adapted.
